title: A tuned rubric judge cleared notes where 1 in 5 still hid a serious error
summary: Across production clinical AI notes, a detailed faithfulness rubric plus deterministic checks passed notes where 1 in 5 clean passes still hid a harm-level error — the standard belongs in expert corrections, not in a frozen rubric.
takeaways: In a high-stakes domain, the errors your judge rubric clears are the ones that hurt the user; keep the quality standard in expert corrections retrieved into the judge's context per output, not frozen in the rubric.

A strong LLM-as-judge with a faithfulness rubric, worked examples and deterministic text checks still let through notes where 1 in 5 clean passes hid a serious error, because verification is only cheap for the spot-the-difference part.

Two other production teams converge on buying expert judgment: physician-authored rubrics and clinician-calibrated judges at Abridge, and error analysis on real logs by the expert you sell to at Allos AI.

sources.title: Sebastian Fox (Composo): Inside 847 production clinical AI notes
Abridge: from ambient documentation to clinical intelligence
Allos AI: parallels in applied vertical AI

body:
## What happened

In a talk published 2026-08-22, Sebastian Fox — a medical doctor now at Composo, which builds evaluation systems for high-stakes domains — [walked through the failures](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yqF6XhzbWBk) his team found in notes from three of the leading production ambient scribes (systems that draft a clinical note from the doctor-patient conversation). Citing the largest real-world study of such notes, he reports roughly 1 in 20 carried an error serious enough to cause significant harm: "that's not theoretical in testing, that's in production on real patients." Nearly 1 in 5 had an important omission, and for most of these systems "there's no adverse event reporting at all."

## Why it matters

Most failures happen with a perfect transcript: the model adds, changes, or omits something, and the hard part is judging which difference matters. Fox reports that a strong LLM-as-judge setup — faithfulness rubric, worked examples, optimized prompts, deterministic text checks — [cleared notes where 1 in 5 clean passes still hid a serious error](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yqF6XhzbWBk). Two talks the same week agree the judge needs the expert: [Abridge](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u6q-byPWUuo), at about 300 US health systems and 100M conversations a year, scores clinician-calibrated judges against physician-authored rubrics, and [Allos AI's Ayush Bhardwaj](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yphdry8ttAQ) says a generic judge jargons its way through a domain it cannot verify.

## How it works

1. **Discover.** [Cluster real production outputs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yqF6XhzbWBk) to find the failure modes you actually have, rather than guessing them on a whiteboard.
2. **Capture.** Record expert clinicians' free-form corrections and their reasoning, not a pass/fail label.
3. **Calibrate.** Retrieve the most relevant past judgments and guidelines into the judge's context per output, so the standard lives in examples instead of a frozen rubric.

> The dangerous failures are the ones that look completely fine on the page.

## The catch

This loop is Fox's proposal, from a vendor that sells evaluation tooling, and his caught-versus-missed error map comes from notes his team generated last week, not an audit of deployed records. It also assumes continuous expert time: someone qualified keeps correcting outputs and explaining why, indefinitely. Price that before you copy it.
